studies.title: Corporate Chairman Vignette
studies.description: Tests whether calling a side effect intentional depends on whether it is harmful or helpful, with a corporate chairman vignette.

studies.title: Military Lieutenant Vignette
studies.description: Repeats the test with a military lieutenant vignette to check the effect is not specific to corporations or environmental harm.

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: Does evaluating a side-effect as good or bad influence whether people call it intentional?
fields.derivation: Summarized from the benchmark ground-truth hypotheses.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: A person’s intuitions as to whether or not a given side-effect was produced 'intentionally' can be influenced by that person’s attitude toward the specific side-effect in question (specifically whether it is good or bad).

fields.value: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 2.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

fields.label: N analysed
fields.value: Experiment 1: 78; Experiment 2: 42 (120 in total).

fields.label: Design type
fields.value: Between-participants: each person reads one version of the vignette.

fields.label: Vignette
fields.value:
The vice-president of a company went to the chairman of the board and said, ‘We are thinking of starting a new program. It will help us increase profits, but it will also harm the environment.’

The chairman of the board answered, ‘I don’t care at all about harming the environment. I just want to make as much profit as I can. Let’s start the new program.’

They started the new program. Sure enough, the environment was harmed.

value.question: Did the chairman intentionally harm the environment?
How much blame the chairman deserved for what he did (on a scale from 0 to 6)?

fields.label: Vignette
fields.value:
The vice-president of a company went to the chairman of the board and said, ‘We are thinking of starting a new program. It will help us increase profits, and it will also help the environment.’

The chairman of the board answered, ‘I don’t care at all about helping the environment. I just want to make as much profit as I can. Let’s start the new program.’

They started the new program. Sure enough, the environment was helped.

value.question: Did the chairman intentionally help the environment?
How much praise the chairman deserved (on a scale from 0 to 6)?

fields.label: Vignette
fields.value:
A lieutenant was talking with a seargent. The lieutenant gave the order: ‘Send your squad to the top of Thompson Hill.’

The seargent said: ‘But if I send my the squad to the top of Thompson Hill, we’ll be moving the men directly into the enemy’s line of fire. Some of them will surely be killed!’

The lieutenant answered: ‘Look, I know that they’ll be in the line of fire, and I know that some of them will be killed. But I don’t care at all about what happens to our soldiers. All I care about is taking control of Thompson Hill.’

The squad was sent to the top of Thompson Hill. As expected, the soldiers were moved into the enemy’s line of fire, and some of them were killed.

value.question: Did the lieutenant intentionally put the soldiers in the line of fire?

fields.label: Vignette
fields.value:
A lieutenant was talking with a seargent. The lieutenant gave the order: ‘Send your squad to the top of Thompson Hill.’

The seargent said: ‘If I send my squad to the top of Thompson Hill, we’ll be taking the men out of the enemy’s line of fire. They’ll be rescued!’

The lieutenant answered: ‘Look, I know that we’ll be taking them out of the line of fire, and I know that some of them would have been killed otherwise. But I don’t care at all about what happens to our soldiers. All I care about is taking control of Thompson Hill.’

The squad was sent to the top of Thompson Hill. As expected, the soldiers were taken out of the enemy’s line of fire, and they thereby escaped getting killed.

value.question: Did the lieutenant intentionally take the soldiers out of the line of fire?

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Between-participants vignette experiments (two experiments).

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Participants in a Manhattan park read a short vignette in which an agent knowingly causes a side effect, then judge whether the agent acted intentionally and how much blame or praise the agent deserves. Two experiments, a corporate and a military scenario.
fields.derivation: Condensed from the benchmark specification and ground truth, not from the PDF text.

fields.label: Task and goal
fields.value: Read one vignette about an agent who knowingly produces a side effect, then answer a Yes/No question on intentionality and rate blame or praise from 0 to 6.

fields.label: Answer to the question
fields.value: Side effects judged bad were called intentional far more often than side effects judged good (82% vs 23% in Experiment 1, 77% vs 30% in Experiment 2).
fields.derivation: Restates the reported percentages from the ground truth as a conclusion.

fields.label: Hypothesis support
fields.value: Both chi-square tests reported in the ground truth are significant in the predicted direction.
fields.derivation: From the reported tests of the harm vs help hypothesis.

fields.label: Mechanism, tested
fields.value: Blame and praise scores correlated with intentionality judgments across both experiments.

fields.label: Mechanism, speculated
fields.value: The asymmetry in blame and praise may be at the root of the asymmetry in applying the concept of intentional action.

fields.label: Replications reported by the paper
fields.value: Experiment 2 repeats Experiment 1 with a military scenario.

fields.label: Steps an agent can perform
fields.value: Reading the vignette and answering the two questions are single-turn text tasks an agent can perform.

fields.label: Roles that can be simulated
fields.value: All original participants. The paper has no confederate or experimenter role to script.

fields.label: Conditions that can be expressed
fields.value: Harm and help vignettes are verbatim text and can be given exactly.

fields.label: Observable outcomes
fields.value: The Yes/No intentionality answer and the 0 to 6 blame or praise rating.

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: How people were assigned to conditions and the order of the two questions are undecided (see open questions). An agent has no experience of the park setting.

issues.title: Choose the assignment procedure
issues.reason: The benchmark specification says random assignment but does not define how it is implemented.
issues.impact: Condition balance and reproducibility depend on this decision.
issues.suggestedAction: Specify allocation, balancing and participant assignment with the agent.

issues.title: Verify question order
issues.reason: The specification lists moral rating before intentionality, but the material JSON lists intentionality first.
issues.suggestedAction: Check the original paper and choose the order before building the study.

issues.title: Background and gap not extracted
issues.reason: The sample was built from the benchmark specification, which does not state the gap the paper addresses.
issues.impact: Section 02 cannot say what prior work left open.
issues.suggestedAction: Read the paper introduction with the agent and add the gap with its page citation.

issues.title: Contribution not extracted
issues.reason: The sample was built from the benchmark files, which do not state the paper's theoretical or practical contribution.
issues.impact: Section 10 cannot say what the finding adds.
issues.suggestedAction: Read the discussion with the agent and add it with its page citation.

issues.impact: Researchers cannot tell what can be re-used.

originalSpecification.title: Intentional Action and Side-Effects in Ordinary Language

participants.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 1.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 2.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

steps: Participants are randomly assigned to either a 'harm condition' or a 'help condition'.
Participants read a vignette (either about a corporate chairman or a military lieutenant) implementing a plan with a known side-effect that the agent claims not to care about.
Participants assess how much blame (in the harm condition) or praise (in the help condition) the agent deserves on a scale from 0 to 6.
Participants answer a categorical (Yes/No) question regarding whether the agent brought about the side-effect intentionally.
